6.227.m: Pārvatī said: / Explain to me in detail the dignity of the words expressing the mantra's meaning, / and the essential nature of the Lord, as well as his manifestations and qualities,
that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, and the divisions of Hari's emanations. / Tell me everything in its true reality, O Lord of all gods!
The Lord said: / Listen, O goddess, I shall explain the essential nature of the Supreme Self, / the assemblage of Hari's manifestations and qualities consisting of his states.
The supreme Puruṣa who is Viṣṇu is declared to be Nārāyaṇa; / he is both the Lord of the worlds and the eternal Supreme Self.
With hands and feet on every side, with eyes on every side, the Lord / contains all worlds, the supreme abodes within himself.

Supporting them, he also stands beyond them and beyond the minds of the wise. / Thus being of manifold forms, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Puruṣa, / possesses a divine, auspicious form for the sake of enjoyment with the sovereign Goddess.
With an immense body, of a form resembling fire, a youth who has attained princehood, Hari / sported with Śrī, the mother of the worlds, like the nectar-rayed moon with its own moonlight.
And this youthful prince, ever young with the sovereign Goddess of the world, / with the loveliness of ten million gods of love, stood in the supreme abode.
The supreme sky is for his enjoyment; the entire universe is for his sport. / The subsistence of Viṣṇu's two realms is through enjoyment and play.
His permanent dwelling is in enjoyment; sometimes he dissolves his sport. / Both enjoyment and sport are sustained by him through his omnipotence.
Three-quarters are pervasive in the supreme abode; one quarter of him was here again. / The three-quartered realm is eternal; the sovereign single quarter is non-eternal.
Eternal is that auspicious form of the Lord abiding in the supreme abode, / imperishable, everlasting, divine, ever resting in youth,
ever enclosed in enjoyment with the sovereign Goddess, with Śrī and Bhūmi. / Indeed, this mother of the universe is eternal, the unfailing Śrī of Viṣṇu.
Just as Viṣṇu is all-pervading, so too is Lakṣmī, O fair-faced one; / the ruler of the entire world, Viṣṇu's wife, ever auspicious,
having hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side, / Nārāyaṇī, mother of the universe, the refuge of the whole world.
Upon whose sidelong glance the entire world, moving and unmoving, depends; / by whose opening and closing of eyes the maintenance and dissolution of the world occur.
The primordial Mahālakṣmī of all, possessing the three guṇas, the supreme sovereign Goddess, / whose nature is both visible and invisible, remains pervading the entire [universe].
Beholding that entire universe void, the supreme sovereign Goddess / filled that entire void with her own splendor.
She is renowned as Lakṣmī, Dharaṇī, and also Nīlādevī; / becoming the foundation of the world, she assumed the form of the earth.
In the form of the essence of water and the like, she herself becomes Nīlā's body; / having attained the state of Lakṣmī, she indeed has the form of wealth and speech.
Thus of divine nature, she, the Śrī of the world, resorted to Hari. / All the varieties of knowledge have the form of Lakṣmī, O fair-faced one.
The entire universe, all of it, is called her body of Śrī; / the beauty, good conduct, and fortune abiding in women / is her form, O daughter of the mountain, residing at the head of all women.
By the wide, intense gaze of whose sidelong glance Brahmā, Śiva, the lord of heaven Mahendra, / the moon, the sun, Kubera, and Agni obtain abundant sovereignty.
Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Vidyā, Mother, Viṣṇu's beloved, the virtuous wife, / Padmālayā, lotus-handed, lotus-eyed, the beauty of the world,
ruler of creatures, eternal, enduring, all-pervading, auspicious, / Viṣṇu's wife, Mahādevī, daughter of the milk ocean, Ramā,
infinite, mother of the world, Bhū, Nīlā, bestower of all happiness, / Rukmiṇī, and likewise Sītā, full of all sacred knowledge, auspicious,
Satī, Sarasvatī, Gaurī, Śānti, Svāhā, Svadhā, Rati, / Nārāyaṇī, of fair hips, ever unfailing to Viṣṇu—
whoever recites these sacred names having risen in the morning, / attains great fortune, and stainless wealth and grain.
The golden-hued, the doe, wearing garlands of gold and silver, / the moon-like, golden Lakṣmī, who never departs from Viṣṇu,
perceivable through fragrance, unassailable, ever thriving, rich in cow dung, / the sovereign Lady of all beings—that Śrī I invoke here.
Thus indeed praised in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, the supreme sovereign Goddess / granted the happiness of all sovereignty to the gods beginning with Śiva.
For she is the ruler of this universe, the eternal wife of Viṣṇu, / upon whose sidelong glance the entire world, moving and unmoving, depends.
Upon whose chest that goddess abides, like radiance in fire, / he indeed is the Lord of all, directly the imperishable, immutable Puruṣa.
He indeed is the glorious Nārāyaṇa, an ocean of the quality of tender affection, / the master, of good character, fortunate, omniscient, omnipotent,
ever having all desires fulfilled, a natural friend and companion, / an ocean of the nectar of compassion, the refuge of all embodied beings,
the giver of the bliss of heaven and liberation, compassionate to devotees: / 'To that glorious Viṣṇu I render all service
in all states, places, times, and the like, to the husband of Kamalā.' / Thus the essential nature being accomplished, one attains blissful servitude.
Having thus understood the meaning of the mantra, one should properly practice devotion to him. / This world, moving and unmoving, has become his servant.
The glorious Nārāyaṇa is the master, the lord and ruler of the worlds, / mother, father, son, relative, dwelling place, refuge, and destination,
possessed of auspicious qualities, the Lord of Śrī, the bestower of the fruits of all desires. / He who is spoken of in the scriptures as without qualities, the Lord of the universe,
is spoken of as devoid of material qualities connected with the base. / Where the falsity of the phenomenal world [is declared] by statements within the domain of the Upaniṣads,
All this that is visible is declared to be impermanent; / here too, the material form of the cosmic egg undergoes destruction.
Indeed, the impermanence of material forms is thus described; / understand this matter, O great goddess, as the manifestation of Hari's material nature.
For the sake of sport, by the God of gods, Viṣṇu, who commands divine play, / with fourteen worlds, with oceans accompanied by continents,
with the four kinds of creatures, and with very lofty mountains, / this delightful cosmic egg, produced from material nature, is filled.
Endowed with ten times each successive quality, enclosed by seven coverings, / time revolves in the form of moments, measures, and the like;
by time alone the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe occurs. / A thousand four-age cycles is indeed a day of Brahmā;
so many years are the night of Brahmā whose birth is from the unmanifest. / But when Brahmā's dissolution arrives, universal destruction takes place.
The cosmic egg and the worlds within it are burned by the fire of time; / likewise, all individual souls are deposited into Viṣṇu's material nature.
The coverings of the cosmic egg dissolve into material nature; / that material nature, the foundation of the whole universe, rests upon Hari.
Through it, the Lord always carries out the creation and dissolution of the universe; / for the sake of sport, māyā composed of the universe was created by the God of gods.
Ignorance, material nature, māyā is always composed of the three qualities; / it is eternal, the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Yoganidrā, Mahāmāyā, material nature endowed with the three qualities, / the unmanifest and the primal matter of Viṣṇu, who transforms in sport.
The creation and dissolution of the universe always arise from material nature alone; / the realm of incalculable material nature is dense darkness, imperishable.
Above, at its boundary, is the Virajā, the eternal, boundless base; / by material nature the entire universe is held in coarse and subtle states.
The states of expansion and contraction are remembered as its creation and dissolution; / in this way, all beings are indeed contained within material nature.
Then all this great [expanse] contained within material nature is empty; / thus is the superior form of the glory consisting of material nature.
Now hear, O daughter of the mountain, about the form of the three-quartered glory: / between primal matter and the supreme ether flows the Virajā river,
auspicious, flowing with waters born of the sweat of the limbs of the Vedas. / Beyond it, in the supreme ether, is the eternal three-quartered manifestation:
deathless, constant, eternal, infinite, the supreme abode, / pure, consisting of pure goodness, divine, the imperishable realm of Brahman,
possessing an imperishable splendor equal to many tens of millions of suns and fires, / consisting of all the Vedas, pure, devoid of creation and dissolution,
countless, unaging, eternal, free from waking, dreaming, and the other states, / golden, the realm of liberation, bringing the bliss and happiness of Brahman,
free from equal or superior, devoid of beginning or end, auspicious, / exceedingly wondrous in splendor, delightful, an eternal ocean of bliss.
Endowed with such qualities is that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; / the sun does not illuminate it, nor the moon, nor fire;

having gone to which they do not return, that is the supreme abode of Hari. / That supreme abode of Viṣṇu is constant, eternal, infallible; / it cannot be described even in hundreds of millions of cosmic eras.
Hari's abode cannot be described by me, nor by the Creator, nor by hosts of chief sages; / in that abode, the Lord who is infallible—he alone knows, or perhaps he knows not.
That imperishable, secret of the Vedas, in which all the gods sat down together— / what will one who does not know that do with the Ṛgveda? Those who know it sit happily united.
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, / imperishable, constant, divine, O goddess, spread out like an eye [in the sky].
It cannot be entered by Brahmā, Rudra, and the other deities; / it is seen by the foremost yogins through knowledge, by the path of scripture.
I, Brahmā, the gods, and the great sages do not fully know it; / having perceived the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, I shall tell you, O lady of good vows.
In Viṣṇu's supreme abode, in that abode of auspicious name, / where cattle with abundant horns dwell, the subjects are exceedingly happy.
Here scripture proclaims that supreme abode of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow disguised as a cowherd; / that supreme abode shines with cattle and cowherds bearing names of bliss.
Sun-colored, beyond darkness, an infallible light, / the realm of Brahman is the support, consisting of pure goodness, eternal.
In this constant abode of common glory and ground, / those two, ever-youthful and eternal Śrī, stood watchful;
for the two youthful sisters, Bhū and Nīlā, are Viṣṇu's beloveds. / Here, the ancient Sādhyas and the eternal Viśvedevas,
they who have attained the realm of heaven, fair to behold, dwell together. / There wise brāhmaṇas, ever wakeful, blaze forth.
To that realm wise brāhmaṇas go, desiring to dwell together; / that supreme abode of Viṣṇu is called liberation.
In it, those freed from bondage attain a blissful abode; / having reached it they do not return: therefore it is called liberation.
Liberation is the supreme, divine abode, deathless, the dwelling of Viṣṇu, / the imperishable, supreme realm, Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal abode.
Eternal, supreme sky, most exalted and timeless— / these are synonymous words for the supreme abode and for Acyuta. / I shall describe in detail the nature of that three-quartered domain of glory.

6.228.m: Glorious Mahādeva said: / Countless worlds belonging to the three-quartered domain of glory are celebrated; / they all consist of pure sattva, designated by the bliss and happiness of brahman.
All are eternal, free from modification, devoid of unworthy passion and the like; / all are golden, pure, possessing the radiance of ten million suns.
All consist of the Veda, divine, free from desire and wrath; / they are served solely by the essence of devotion to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
They continuously take shelter in the happiness filled with the singing of the Sāmans; / they all have the nature of the five Upaniṣads, possessing the lustre of the Veda.
They are filled with divine men and women consisting of the Vedas; / they are adorned with lakes rich in water that is the sole essence of the Vedas.
They are accompanied by immovable beings possessing the forms of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth. / It is not possible for me to describe the entire extent of those worlds.
The interval between the Virajā and the supreme sky is taught to be solitary; / that place is to be enjoyed by those who worship the unmanifest brahman.
Giving the bliss and happiness born of the experience of one's own self, it is the solitary state; / it is called the highest good, nirvāṇa, kaivalya, and liberation.

Those devoid of devotion to the feet of the Lord of Śrī, whose pleasure is only in sense enjoyment, / those of little understanding desire that liberation devoid of happiness. / But the great-souled, highly fortunate ones who serve the Lord's feet
go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which grants the bliss of brahman, / crowded with various realms—that Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Hari.
Enclosed by surrounding walls, aerial cars, and palaces made of jewels, / in its midst is the divine city celebrated as Ayodhyā.
It is enclosed by walls and arched gates adorned with variegated jewels and gold, / furnished with four gates and surrounded by jeweled gateways.
Guarded by the gatekeepers Caṇḍa and the others, and by Kumuda and the rest: / Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are at the eastern gate; Bhadra and Subhadra are at the southern;
Jaya and Vijaya are at the western; Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are at the northern. / Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana,
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita— / these are proclaimed as the guardians of the directions in this city, O fair-faced one.
It is filled with rows of houses resembling ten million fires, / accompanied by divine men and women of perpetual youth and eternal nature.
The inner palace of the Lord in the center of the city is charming, / equipped with a wall of jewels and adorned with jeweled arched gateways,
furnished with aerial cars, principal mansions, and many palaces, / decorated on all sides by divine groups of Apsarases and women.
In the middle is a divine pavilion, the royal assembly, exceedingly high, / attended by a thousand ruby columns, made of jewels, and auspicious.
Pervaded by divine liberated beings, adorned with the singing of the Sāmans; / in its middle is a delightful, auspicious throne consisting of all the Vedas,
perpetually surrounded by the deities Dharma and the others, who are of the nature of the Vedas, / with Dharma, Knowledge, Great Sovereign Power, and Dispassion as the bodily forms of its legs,
perpetually surrounded in order by the forms of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas. / Śakti, the foundational power, and the consciousness-power, Sadāśivā,
are celebrated as the powers of the deities such as Dharma. / Fire, Sun, and Moon dwell in the center there;
Kūrma, the Serpent King, and Garuḍa, the lord of the three Vedas, / the meters, and all the mantras have assumed the form of the throne.
It is traditionally remembered as the divine yogic throne consisting of all syllables; / in its center is an eight-petaled lotus, radiant like the rising sun.
In the center of it, on the pericarp, which is Sāvitrī, O fair-looking one, / seated together with His consort, the Lord of gods, the Supreme Person,
dark like the petal of a blue lotus, possessing the radiance of ten million suns, / youthful, tender, endowed with soft limbs,
resembling a blooming red lotus, with soft lotus feet, / wide-awake, lotus-eyed, marked with a pair of vine-like beautiful eyebrows,
having a handsome nose, fine cheeks, and a lotus-face with beautiful ears, / having teeth resembling pearls, with smiling coral lips,
resembling the full moon, with a lotus face gently smiling, / shining with two ear-rings having the color of the morning sun,
adorned with sleek, dark, curly locks of hair, / having His hair tied in a braid enriched with mandāra and pārijāta flowers,
adorned with the Kaustubha jewel resembling the thousand-rayed sun rising at dawn, / shining with a conch-like neck adorned with necklaces and a gold garland,
shining with raised, plump shoulders resembling a lion's shoulders, / adorned with four plump, round, and long arms,
ornamented with rings, bracelets, and armlets, / and with excellent ornaments like the Kaustubha, resembling ten million morning suns,
His broad chest resplendent, decorated with the forest garland, / adorned with the navel-lotus, the birthplace of the Creator,
attired in fine yellow garments resembling morning sunlight, / shining with anklets on feet variegated with various jewels,
having rows of nails resembling the moon accompanied by moonlight, / Acyuta, a treasure of beauty with the loveliness of ten million gods of love,
His body anointed with divine sandalwood paste, adorned with a divine garland, / shining with raised arms holding the conch and the discus,
and likewise with the other two hands displaying the gesture of granting boons and the gesture of fearlessness. / Seated on His left side is the goddess Mahālakṣmī, the Great Sovereign,
golden-hued, deer-like, wearing a garland of gold and silver, / endowed with all auspicious marks, Her body showing the onset of youth,
endowed with jeweled earrings, with dark, curly hair, / Her limbs smeared with divine sandalwood paste, adorned with divine flowers,
Her beautiful locks of hair adorned with mandāra, ketakī, and jātī flowers, / with beautiful eyebrows, a fine nose, beautiful hips, and plump, prominent breasts,
resembling the full moon, with a lotus face gently smiling, / shining with earrings possessing the color of the morning sun,
having the luster of molten gold, adorned with molten gold ornaments, / equipped with four hands, adorned with golden lotuses,
rich in various variegated gems, with a garland of golden lotuses, / adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and rings,
adorned with a pair of raised lotuses held by two arms, / Her hands adorned with gold holding a citron.
Thus with the eternal, inseparable Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign Lord / continuously rejoices in the eternal supreme sky.
On either side, Dharaṇī and Nīlā are seated upon auspicious seats; / and at the tips of the petals in the eight directions are the powers Vimalā and the rest:
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and also Yogā, / Prahvī, Satyā, and likewise Īśānā—the powers of the Supreme Self.
Holding divine chowries possessing the radiance of the moon, / endowed with all auspicious marks, they rejoice in their lord, Acyuta.
Five hundred heavenly Apsarases, women / who dwell in the inner apartments, adorned with all ornaments,
All with lotuses in their hands, radiant as ten million fires, / endowed with every auspicious mark, their faces resembling the cool-rayed moon—
Surrounded by them, the King, the Supreme Person, shone forth, / along with the lord of gods, Ananta, the lord of birds, the commanders of the army, and others,
Surrounded by other attendants, eternal and liberated beings, / the Person rejoices with Ramā, delighting in enjoyments and sovereignty.
Thus this Lord of Vaikuṇṭha shines in the supreme abode. / I shall speak to you, auspicious mountain-born goddess, of the realms of his various emanations.
To the east in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha is the mansion of Vāsudeva; / in the south-east is the world of Lakṣmī, and in the south is the abode of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
In the south-west is the realm of Sarasvatī, and in the west that of Pradyumna; / in the north-west is the realm of Rati, and in the north is the domain of Aniruddha.
In the north-east is the world of Śānti; this is recorded as the first enclosure. / Then in succession are these twenty-four realms beginning with Keśava;
They are declared to be the auspicious second enclosure of Vaikuṇṭha. / The realms beginning with the Fish and the Tortoise are the auspicious third enclosure.
The realms of Satya, Acyuta, Ananta, Durgā, Viṣvaksena, Gajānana, / and the treasures Śaṅkha and Padma are the auspicious fourth enclosure.
The realms of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, in the great intermediate directions, / and of Sāvitrī, the Lord of Birds, Dharma, and Makha,
Are declared to be the imperishable fifth enclosure, consisting of all speech. / The conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, Śārṅga bow, and plough,
And the pestle—these realms, endowed with all weapons and missiles, / are declared to be the imperishable sixth enclosure, composed of mantras and weapons.
The directions of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, / Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna are remembered by sages as the seventh enclosure.
The Sādhyas, the Maruts, and likewise the Viśvedevas, / and whatever other dwellers of heaven there are, all exist eternally in the supreme realm.
In this material world, the lords of the thirty gods are indeed non-eternal. / 'They, the great ones, attain the firmament,' so indeed says the Vedic revelation.
Thus the omnipresent Lord shines in the supreme realm with eternal liberated souls dedicated to divine enjoyments, / and with His divine consorts.
Neither the sun illuminates it, nor the moon, nor fire; / having gone there, yogins of strict vows do not return.
Those who are devoted exclusively to the two-fold mantra indeed go to that imperishable [abode], / not by study of the Vedas, sacrifices, gifts, nor auspicious vows,
nor by austerities of fasting, nor by ritual actions; / by the single two-fold mantra alone and likewise by unswerving devotion,
that eternal, ancient realm is to be attained indeed through surrender. / Pārvatī said: You have well described the nature of the supreme heaven, O Lord.
Being stationed eternally in the supreme sky, how has He resided in the realm of nature? / For what reason? What was the purpose of His playful sport?
The Supreme Lord resides in a realm of pure sattva; / how did the Lord stay with a manifestation mixed with rajas and tamas?
Rudra said: In His threefold manifestation, the Lord, the Supreme Master, through His divine power, / to be enjoyed solely by the eternally liberated, that all-pervading One rejoices constantly.
To that Lord, Mahāmāyā, Prakṛti, the refuge of the universe, / folding her hands in reverence, offered praise to the Supreme Lord.
Mahāmāyā said: Salutations to You, the abode of the three worlds! Salutations to You, whose form is the universe! / Salutations to You, the ancient One, the cause of the universe's arising!
To the Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā, and salutations to Nārāyaṇa! / Salutations to You, the Blessed Lord, to Vāsudeva, wielder of the Śārṅga bow!
Salutations to Viṣṇu, victorious, whose form is all the gods! / Salutations to You of a thousand forms, to Ananta! Salutations to You!
To Acyuta, the changeless, whose nature is pure sattva, / whose true form is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, salutations again and again!
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Wisdom, to the Supreme Self, / to You, the Self of all beings, and the refuge of all beings!
To Brahman, to Light, to You, salutations to You whose form is the universe! / Salutations to You who dwell in purity, to the Haṃsa, and to the Supreme One!

To Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Rudra, and to the sustainer of all beings; / to Hayagrīva, radiant, to Time, to Hari, salutations! / Salutations to You, O Sacrifice-Person, whose nature is the oblations to gods and ancestors!
Salutations to Prajāpati, to the sun of auspicious radiance, / and to Agni, consumer of offerings, salutations to that embodiment of sacrifice!
Salutations to You, the progenitor, the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution! / Salutations to the One known through the Vedānta, whose nature is fourfold!
To Brahmā, to Viṣṇu, salutations to You, and to Śaṅkara! / Salutations to You who possess the three guṇas, the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution!
Salutations to You who are devoid of guṇas, dwelling inside all beings! / Salutations to that unmanifest Viṣṇu, witness of the world!
To Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Śrī, the embodiment of the complete six qualities, / filled with infinite virtues, salutations to the granter of all desires!
Salutations to You, Vāsudeva, whose form comprises the five states! / Salutations, salutations to You who take the form of five and nine vyūha divisions!
Salutations to the Sacrificial Boar, to Govinda, salutations again and again! / To the changeless, the pure, the opponent of all faults!
Salutations to Rāma, to Kṛṣṇa, salutations to You, to Narasiṃha! / Salutations to You, Keśava, remover of the afflictions of the worlds!
You alone are the refuge of all the worlds, O Supreme Person! / Be pleased, O God of gods, for the welfare of all the worlds!
Remaining within me, all sentient beings are without support, without refuge, / devoid of bodies, formless, bereft of all senses,
destitute of all ritual practice, constantly experiencing sorrow. / You ought to grant them worlds and bodies, O Keśava!
Fashion the realm of playful sport, O omniscient One, as before: / the entire universe, both conscious and unconscious, moving and unmoving!
Behold it deluded by me, O Supreme Lord, for the purpose of sport! / Create the cosmic egg of matter together with me, O Supreme Person!
Having cast righteousness and unrighteousness, pleasure and pain into that transmigratory flow, / presiding over me, You should engage in sport without delay!
Śrī Mahādeva said: Thus addressed by that goddess, Māyā, the Supreme Lord, / entering into that Māyā, set about creating the universe.
He who is declared to be the spirit of nature is none other than Acyuta here; / that very Blessed Viṣṇu indeed entered into Prakṛti.
From Prakṛti He created the cosmic intellect, the support of the Mahat and primary matter; / from this Mahat Puruṣa, the ego arose.
From that ego arose the triad of guṇas; / from the three guṇas, the creator of the universe brought forth the subtle elements.
From the subtle elements arose the gross elements at that very moment. / First the syllable Oṃ was born from Brahman consisting of the three guṇas.
From space arose wind; from wind fire was born; / from fire the waters were produced, and from the waters the earth is considered [to arise].
The gross elements beginning with space were created, each possessing one more quality [than the previous]: / sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities.
Having created those qualities increasing by one, taking them up, the Great Lord / combined them and created the vast cosmic egg; / and within it He created the worlds, which are fourteen in number.
In it the Supreme Person created the gods beginning with Brahmā, / and the fourfold [classes of beings]: divine, animal, human, and stationary.
Thus was the great creation made by Him, O lotus-eyed one! / There, in accordance with their past actions, into wombs of gods and others,
the souls previously situated in Prakṛti indeed come forth.

6.229.m: Pārvatī said: Tell me in detail the unsurpassed creation of the gods, / how the eternal, best dwellers of heaven beginning with Brahmā were born, / and tell me in detail about the incarnations of the Lord!
Rudra said: Space, wind, fire, water, and earth were created in due order; / in their midst Brahmā created the ocean of fathomless water.
When this had become a single cosmic ocean, Hari, on a banyan leaf of water-māyā, / taking up all beings, entered into yogic sleep.
Desiring to create the universe, He entered into yogic sleep; / with that Māyā the slayer of Madhu took delight for a long time.
Within her, He brought forth the unsurpassed Soul of Time, / consisting of units such as kalās and kāṣṭhās, taking the forms of fortnights, months, and so forth.
At that time, from Hari's navel, a lotus bud-like in shape, / blossoming, radiant, the seed of the entire world,
arose, and there Brahmā of great intellect was born. / Desiring to create the universe, impelled by the quality of rajas, / he praised the Supreme Lord lying in yogic sleep.
Brahmā said: Salutations be to You, Viṣṇu, the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, / the adornment of the universe's ornament, the glorious One whose form is the cosmos!
Salutations to the deity benevolent to Brahmins, who works welfare for cows and Brahmins, / for the welfare of the world, to Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, salutations again and again!
To the form of Pradhāna and Time, to the Puruṣa, and to the Sovereign Lord; / salutations to the One whose form is the manifested universe and whose nature is free from manifold manifestation!
To Nārāyaṇa, to the All, salutations to the Lord of the All, / to the Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā, to Brahman, to the Supreme Self!
Salutations be unto Vāsudeva, who is the universal form, the wielder of the bow Śārṅga, / the lord of the three Vedas, Hari, having the essential nature of the Lord of the Universe.
Salutations to you, who are replete with infinite auspicious qualities! / And the entire world sleeps when you, identical with the world, are asleep.
The whole world, moving and unmoving, is encompassed within creation, O Lord of the Universe; / you alone are the cause, the agent, and the effect produced from the three guṇas.

6.229.d:
स्रष्टाध्याताविधाताचत्वमेवपरमेश्वरः
जागर्षिशुद्धसत्वस्थस्तवनिद्राकुतःप्रभो
देवत्वयि स्थितालोकाः समाधिष्ठाः सनातनाः
6.229.m: You alone are the creator, the meditator, the ordainer, and the Supreme Lord. / Established in pure sattva, you remain awake; how could there be sleep for you, O Lord? / O God, the eternal worlds are situated in you, established in absorption.
Śiva said: / Addressed thus by Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Lord, / arose from that bed, released from yogic sleep.
Restraining that yogic sleep, he set about creating the world— / the incomprehensible god, the Lord of the worlds, Acyuta, at that very moment.
Having reflected, that Puruṣa then created the entire world, / indeed, all the worlds, and the golden egg situated in the waters.
The seven continents ending at the oceans, the earth with its mountains, / together with the shell of the single egg, the Lord created in his navel-lotus.
And inside that egg, Hari, the Lord, made an abode. / Then, someone meditated upon Nārāyaṇa with a mind focused on the Supreme Self.
At the end of meditation, from his forehead a drop of sweat arose; / that drop, in the shape of a bubble, instantly fell upon the earth.
From that very bubble, I was born, O fair-faced one— / three-eyed, holding a trident in my hand, and adorned with a crown of matted hair.
‘What shall I do?’ I said with humility to the Lord of the gods. / Then the god Nārāyaṇa, filled with joy, spoke to me:
‘O Rudra, you shall bring about the terrible-looking destruction of the two worlds, / directly through a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, for the sake of dissolution, O fair-faced one.’
Therefore from Nārāyaṇa, O goddess, I was born as a terrifying being. / But having appointed me to destruction, Janārdana once again
created from his eyes the moon and the sun, the dispellers of darkness; / wind and the directions from his ears, and Indra and Agni from his mouth.
From his nostrils the lotus-eyed one created Varuṇa and Mitra, / and from his arms all the gods, along with the Sādhyas and the hosts of Maruts.
From all his hair-pores arose jewels and herbs; / on his skin were mountains and oceans, as well as cattle and other beasts.
The brāhmaṇa was created from his mouth, and the kṣatriya likewise from his arms; / the vaiśya from his thighs, and the śūdra was born thus from his feet.
Having thus created the entire world, which remained inanimate, / the Lord of the gods took his stand inside it in his universal form.
For without that power of Hari, there is no manifestation; / therefore the eternal Viṣṇu alone is the life-breath of the entire world.
He alone, being the unmanifest form, remains as the Supreme Self. / Brahmā himself sets in motion creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
This eternal Vāsudeva, replete with the six divine qualities, / manifests his own form from the three guṇas in four ways as the universe.
The Lord in the form of Pradyumna, endowed with all sovereignty, / of Brahmā, the Lords of Creatures, of time, and of living beings,
having attained inner control, properly performs creation indeed. / Then he gave the Vedas along with legendary histories to that great-souled one.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is a portion of Pradyumna; / born of a portion, he carries out all the creation and maintenance of the world.
And the Lord Aniruddha, endowed with power and splendor, / of the Manus, the kings, time, and living beings—
the Lord effects their maintenance, relying on his state as inner controller. / Saṃkarṣaṇa is Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with knowledge and strength.
Relying on his state as inner controller of time, of all beings, / of Rudra, and of Yama, the Lord dissolves the universe.
Thus, in the state of the inner controller, is the inner control of the Self; / [then] the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, and the dwarf.
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha, and Kalkin—these ten: / these indeed are the manifested states of Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
In Nṛsiṃha, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa, the six divine qualities are proclaimed. / But the supreme state of the Lord is like a lamp produced from a lamp.
Hear of that state of this Hari, O auspicious daughter of the mountain: / Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme world, the incomparable realm of Viṣṇu,
Śvetadvīpa in its essential nature, and the supreme Ocean of Milk. / Thus the fourfold manifestation has been correctly described by the great seers.
In the midst of the water-enclosure lies the auspicious Vaikuṇṭha, the primal cause, / resembling millions of fires, entirely righteous and imperishable,
abounding with trees fragrant with mandāra fragrance, and surrounded by divine fires, / made of diverse gems, and accompanied by millions of celestial cars.
That which is called the supreme abode is established with such characteristics. / In that city of Vaikuṇṭha, radiant with various gems,
in the center is Devajayārāma, a delightful and incomparable city, / furnished with four gates and equipped with golden ramparts and archways,
guarded by doorkeepers such as Caṇḍa and Kumuda and others, / and covered with rows of divine houses made of various jewels,
extending on all sides for five lotuses of yojanas, / and surrounded by millions of palaces a thousand yojanas high,
adorned with divine men and women of blooming youth; / and the women and men in it are adorned with all auspicious marks,
possessing forms equal to Śrī Viṣṇu, adorned with all ornaments, / clothed in divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine sandalwood.
There they rejoice, O Lord of the gods, through devotion pleasing to their souls; / perfected through the eight-syllable mantra, endowed with sixteenfold devotion,
and having entered that abode, they rejoice according to their heart's desire. / Having gone to this [realm], they do not return, dwelling together with Viṣṇu.
Indeed, united with Viṣṇu through an unbroken self, those auspicious, / wise ones perpetually attain happiness equal to his.
Wherever they enter the realms of Hari, those of pure heart, / like beings dwelling in heaven, do not attain heaven again.
Just as the son of Sumitrā and Bharata, and just as Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, / so they too are born in Satyaloka as they wish.
By that very means they will go again to that eternal, supreme abode; / for Vaiṣṇavas there is no birth bound by karma.
For the wise state that attending upon Viṣṇu is liberation; / servitude to the Lord of immortals is not proclaimed to be bondage.
Released from all bondage, the servants of Hari are free from affliction. / The worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are characterized by return [to rebirth];
they consist of karmic bondage, grant pain, friendlessness, and fear, / yield the fruit of great exertion, O goddess, and are causes of birth and destruction.
The enjoyment of pleasures for men is like eating food mixed with poison. / Seeing mortals situated in heaven when their karma is exhausted,
the gods become angry and cast them down into saṃsāra, the bondage of effects. / Therefore, O goddess, the happiness of heaven is achieved by much labor;
transitory, crooked, and mingled with sorrow, the yogin should abandon it; / he should constantly remember Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the flood of all sorrows.
Merely by the utterance of the name, they attain the supreme state. / Therefore, O Gaurī, the wise person should pray for the realm of Viṣṇu.
With unswerving devotion one should worship the Lord, the ocean of compassion. / Possessing all knowledge and virtues, he surely protects; there is no doubt.
Therefore, having chanted the eight-syllable mantra, which brings supreme joy and auspiciousness, / one attains the supreme realm of Viṣṇu, which fulfills all desires.
On that jewel-encrusted couch, radiant as a thousand suns, / seated on a divine celestial chariot, the blessed Hari shone.
And there on the golden pedestal supported by the supporting power and others, / made of diverse jewels, divine, possessing diverse colors,
On that eight-petalled lotus, the auspicious abode of the mantra's syllables, / in its delightful pericarp bearing the auspicious seed-syllable of Lakṣmī,
On that seat resembling in splendor ten million rising morning suns, / the divine, glorious Nārāyaṇa was seated upon the lotus seat.
At his right side, the golden Mother of the universe, / holding divine fly-whisks, adorned with divine garlands and ornaments,
Holding a vessel of wealth, a citron, and a golden lotus in her hands; / and on his left side the goddess Earth, with the radiance of blue lotus petals,
Endowed with various ornaments, adorned with wondrous garments; / she held two delightful red lotuses with her raised arms,
And with her other two arms the goddess held a pair of grain vessels. / Holding divine fly-whisks, the powers beginning with Vimalā,
Seated on the tips of the petals, adorned with every auspicious mark; / and in their midst sat the blessed Hari, Acyuta,
With hands bearing conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with divine ornaments, / adorned with ornaments such as armlets, bracelets, and necklaces,
Splendid with earrings shining like the morning thousand-rayed sun, / the Supreme Lord served by the previously mentioned eternal thirty gods.
He dwells in the city of Vaikuṇṭha, eternal and true, possessing enjoyments. / For the wise who have perfected the glorious eight-syllable mantra,
That realm of Viṣṇu can be attained, not by others by any means. / Thus has the first emanation been related to you, O fair-faced one.
Hear of the second realm of Viṣṇu; I shall describe it, O faithful to vows, / which is known as eternal, celebrated as the foremost realm of Viṣṇu.
That vast, holy realm, pure, composed of goodness, auspicious, / illuminated simultaneously as if by a thousand midday suns,
Even at the end of a kalpa that supreme realm never dissolves. / Even by myself, Brahmā, and the other gods, it cannot be seen.
It is completely filled all around with groves of wish-fulfilling trees, / endowed with oblong ponds filled with nectar-like water,
Beautified with divine lotuses of gold and gems, / surrounded by millions of divine ornaments glowing like water, fire, and sun,
Ceaselessly filled with Sāman hymns and the warbling of cuckoos and other birds, / and adorned with fragrant trees borne by wind and airborne chariots,
Filled with divine men and women less than sixteen years of age, / rich with the splendor of all auspicious marks, with divine wishing-tree ornaments.
There in delightful regions and places, the women / worshipped the Lord of the Lotus along with their joyful husbands.
They continually enjoy the bliss obtainable by his grace; / they sing of the supreme joy, the great deed of Kṛṣṇa.
Lotus-eyed, with lotuses in their hands, auspicious, resembling Lakṣmī, / endowed with divine garlands and garments, the fair women were sporting.
Bearing conch, discus, mace, and lotus, adorned with ornaments, / wearing garlands and yellow garments, the men resided there.
From mutual touch as women and men disport there, / the blissful taste of devotion to Hari increases day by day.
In its midst is the delightful, splendid inner apartment of Vāsudeva, / supplied with sandal, agallochum, camphor, and saffron water,
Adorned on all sides with various flower-chariots and the like; / in its midst, in the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree, on a lotus seat,
On a wondrous, smooth couch covered with auspicious coverings, / rich with the supreme beauty of divine fragrances and accessories of various flowers,
Seated on that charming, divine seat together with Śrī, / along with the supreme goddess, is the eternal Lord of gods, Vāsudeva,
Resembling ten million moons, adorned with divine ornaments, / his face graced by a pair of bright golden, smooth nostrils,
Radiant with glossy, long, exquisitely lovely cheeks, / endowed with dark curly hair, his eyes like red lotus petals,
His crest adorned with mandāra, ketakī, jātī, and water lilies, / his lips shining like glossy bimba fruits, his lotus face softly smiling,
Shining with a row of teeth having the luster of priceless pearls, / his limbs smeared with yellowish sandal, marked with a musk tilaka,
Adorned with four long arms and raised shoulders, / resplendent with sprout-like hands resembling China rose flowers,
And adorned with the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha on his broad chest.
Adorned with divine garlands of pearls radiating great beauty, / wrapped in a yellow garment that has the radiance of the morning sun,
Resplendent with lotus petals, wearing ruby anklets, / gleaming with rows of nails that shine like the spotless moon,
With delicate, bright lotus-like hands and feet resembling red water-lilies, / his pair of arms adorned with the Pāñcajanya conch and the discus,
Embracing Śrī's body to his chest with his other two [arms], / he shines like a dark cloud touched by a flashing streak of lightning.
His lotus-like feet are delicate and auspicious like fine Jāmbūnada gold; / here plays the eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord of gods.
She, resembling molten gold, adorned with all ornaments, / adorned with very glossy, dark curly locks, glowing like the moon,
Beautified with divine flowers such as Mandāra and Pārijāta, / richly adorned with ear-ornaments, the ends of her curls like swarms of bees,
Pressing against Hari's chest with her full, elevated breasts, / adorned with ornaments such as armlets, bracelets, and necklaces,
Possessing full youthful vigor, eternally the beauty of all worlds, / she plays there constantly with her husband, the Lord of the worlds.
It is that very Vāsudeva who enchants all living beings; / he plays in this world of all [beings], granting all desires to men.
Here eight energies, forms of Lakṣmī, stand all around: / Ramā, Rukmiṇī, Sītā, Padmā, Padmālayā, Śivā,
Sulakṣaṇā, and virtuous [Suśīlā], bestowing love and delight. / Likewise, with weapons such as the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and the Śārṅga bow,
Arranged in the shape of a lotus all around, they protect that world. / Thus, O fair-faced one, has this second form been properly explained to you
In brief by me, for it cannot be told in full detail. / Those who chant the twelve-syllable mantra that brings happiness,
They attain eternal, imperishable, and constant auspiciousness. / Not by study of the Vedas, nor by sacrifices, nor by vows, nor by fasts,
Can Viṣṇu's realm ever be reached anywhere without servitude [to him]. / Therefore, with an undistracted mind, one should practice devoted servitude to Hari.
One attains supreme perfection that releases one from the bondage of karma. / Thus, O goddess, the second imperishable manifestation is recounted.
Now hear the third supreme manifestation, which I shall tell, O Pārvatī: / on the northern shore of the ocean of water, in Śvetadvīpa, O highly intelligent one,
For the sake of appearing to the yogins, Sanaka and the other great souls: / Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana,
And Sanatkumāra, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha— / these seven sons of Brahmā, yogins of immense power,
Detached from all enjoyments, pure, ever having the quality of sattva, / enjoying solely the delight born from the sight of the Blessed One,
And Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and others who reside in Śvetadvīpa— / for the purpose of granting them a vision, Hari is present there.
In Śvetadvīpa, resembling ten million white moons, blazing with various jewels, / frequented by great yogins, and free from fear,
There are delightful gardens there resembling the Pārijāta, / filled with Saṃtānaka creepers, adorned with sandalwood trees,
Endowed with blooming lotuses and water-lilies, accompanied by various reservoirs of water. / In its center is a charming city, auspicious, named Airāvatī,
Adorned with divine aerial cars made of various gems, / filled with divine men and women, crowded with many mansions.
In its center is a charming inner apartment, filled with wish-fulfilling jewel-trees, / surrounded by many lofty palaces that resemble the morning sun.
In its center is a divine pavilion, adorned with jewels and gold, / fragrant with the perfumes of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron,
Decorated with canopies rich in the beauty of various blossoms, / crowded with divine apsarases, and beautified by the singing of Sāman chants.
In the middle is a throne there, radiant like the sun and fire; / upon it is an eight-petaled lotus, like a second lunar disc.
Seated on the pericarp in its center is Janārdana, / resembling pure Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with pearl necklaces,
Having four hands holding the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and spear, / adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings,
Resplendent with a pair of feet resembling golden lotuses, / gleaming with rows of white nails like Saṃtānaka flowers,
Shining with the form and youth of sixteen years of age, / having on the broad expanse of his forehead an ūrdhvapuṇḍra mark
Drawn with fragrant saffron, adorned with a parting line of hair, / well wrapped in white cloth resembling the foam of churned nectar,
Beautified with a pair of bright pearl earrings, / seated in the lotus posture, his form enchanting the whole world.
Seated upon his left thigh is the goddess, possessing a divine form, / Lakṣmī, matching him in good conduct, excellent qualities, and the like,
Resembling the filaments of a lotus, graced with early youth, / endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with molten gold,
Wearing divine garlands and garments, with dark curly hair, / resplendent with four arms, adorned with armlets and bracelets,
Shining with pearl necklaces, her hair adorned with Mandāra flowers, / with delicate nostrils, gleaming with beautiful teeth,
Bearing a musk tilaka, a pearl adorning the tip of her nose, / with full, high breasts resembling golden water-jars,
Her limbs smeared with divine saffron, adorned with a garland of lotuses, / [holding] a vessel of garments, a citron, a mirror, and a golden lotus
In her lotus hands, the goddess who grants the desires of the heart. / Equal to her are these energies that surround Hari there:
Īśāvāsyā, Mahādevī, Jāhnavī, Kamalālayā, / Sāvitrī, Sarvagā, and Padmā—these are proclaimed as the energies;
Śraddhā, Medhā, Dhṛti, Prajñā, Dhāraṇā, and Śānti, / Śruti, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Medhā, Vṛddhi, Buddhi, and Manīṣiṇī—
These female servants of Śrī are declared to carry out all her tasks. / Deities such as Ananta and Vainateya are his eternal attendants;
The Sādhyas and the hosts of Maruts, eternal deities, serve him. / In palaces, in aerial cars, in groves, and in cities,
Delighted with the pleasures obtained through his grace, / they play constantly and eternally, free from what is contemptible and futile.
Those who repeat the mantra of Viṣṇu, always filled with faith, / and those engaged in the vow of the twelfth day go to his imperishable abode.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by gifts, nor by sacrifices, nor even by vows, / is it possible to attain the eternal world of Viṣṇu, O daughter of the mountain.
Men can attain the abode of Viṣṇu only by undivided devotion; / therefore, one should always worship the god Janārdana with devotion.
Constantly meditating, one should repeat the mantra and sing merely his name; / with devotion one should offer oblations and libations to the all-pervading giver of all desires.
Thus the third manifestation, the essential nature of the Supreme Self, / has been declared to you, O woman of beautiful hips, just as told by the ancients.
Next I will explain the fourth, supreme manifestation. / To protect the inhabitants of heaven, the Supreme Lord,
Resembling ten million nectared moons, in the Ocean of Milk / adorned by the thousand-eyed [Indra] and covered by Puraṃdara along with his hosts,
On that extensive, auspicious couch of Ananta he lies, / seated on a celestial seat: Padmanābha, Acyuta, Hari,
resembling a dark-blue raincloud, with eyes as broad as lotus petals, / resplendent with a diadem radiant as ten million suns,
resplendent with two celestial ear-rings gleaming with diverse jewels, / wrapped in a yellow garment that has the radiance of the morning sun,
adorned with soles of hands and feet lovely as gleaming red lotuses, / resplendent with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and rings,
holding the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and sword in his hands, / resplendent with wish-granting trees rich in fine flowers, fruits, and branches,
adorned with a navel-lotus, the source of birth and death for the universe, / his limbs smeared with Haricandana sandal, decorated with all ornaments,
having his hair arranged into very glossy, dark, wavy braids / with charming celestial blossoms of Mandāra, Pārijāta, and others,
shining with a pair of smooth, raised, shapely nose, shoulders, and knees, / resplendent with anklets on his feet rich in jewels and branches of coral,
gleaming with rows of nails bright as the unblemished moon, / his lotus mouth bearing red lips resembling the Aśoka flower,
resplendent with rows of teeth lustrous as priceless pearls, / beautified by a smiling face resembling the full moon,
having attained youth, glorious, gleaming with delicate limbs, / a refuge for all the worlds, bestowing the fruit of all the worlds.
Equal to him is the goddess in beauty, conduct, virtues, and the like, / resembling molten gold, adorned with molten gold ornaments,
youthful, endowed with beauty, charm, luster, good conduct, and virtues, / wrapped in an auspicious garment resembling the foam of the Milk Ocean,
her hair adorned with Mandāra, Ketakī, and Jātī flowers, / marked with a musk tilaka, beautified by a jewel in the parting of her hair,
rich in great beauty of various colors, adorned with ear-ornaments, / radiant as coral, with a gentle smile on red lips,
resplendent with glossy curls of hair resembling intoxicated bees, / slender-waisted, broad-eyed, with full, elevated breasts,
shining with four arms, decorated with all ornaments; / with her two raised hands the goddess held an auspicious pair of golden lotuses.
embracing her husband tightly with her other two [hands], / continuously looking upon the gods with side-glances.
O auspicious one, those gods, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras, / seated in celestial chariots, who are constantly gazed upon by that goddess, are blessed.
Filled with tears of joy, they constantly sing to the goddess. / When being oppressed by the Daiteyas, the gods, headed by Brahmā and Rudra,
praised the Lord there, and he granted freedom from fear to the gods. / Having granted freedom from fear to the gods, Hari, the lord of all gods,
began to slay the Rākṣasas for the protection of the universe. / Thus the fourth emanation of Hari has been told to you, O sinless one.
What else do you desire to hear? That I shall speak, O fair-faced one! / You are blessed, your purpose is accomplished, and you are devoted to Puruṣottama.

6.230.m: Pārvatī said: / O Lord, Madhusūdana, the lord of gods, having slain the Rākṣasas— / in what form [did he do so]? You ought to explain that properly.
And the manifestation, grosser in size, in the forms of the Fish, the Tortoise, and the like— / relate that at length, O Maheśvara, out of love for me.
Mahādeva said: / Listen with a calm mind, O goddess, and I will explain the divine manifestation, / the forms of Hari, such as the Fish and the Tortoise, consisting of incarnations.
Just as a lamp is produced from a lamp, so it will be [here]: / the supreme state of the Supreme Lord, possessing emanations, manifestations, and so forth.
The auspicious incarnations of the Lord have been spoken of as having diverse forms; / the consecrated images of the Lord are the divine manifestations of the Supreme Self.
Indeed, by the lordship over creatures, Brahmā was a sovereign emperor of supreme celebration. / [He created] Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Dakṣa, and Kardama,
Pulastya, Pulaha, Giriśa, and Kratu— / these are declared, in due order, as the nine lords of creatures.
There, the venerable Marīci begot Kaśyapa. / Kaśyapa had four wives, O you of fair appearance:
Aditi, Diti, Kadru, and Vinatā. / Aditi gave birth to the gods of fair appearance;
and Diti [gave birth to] the Rākṣasas, sons belonging to the quality of darkness, very mighty Asuras: / Śambūka, Hayagrīva, the greatly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa,
Hiraṇyakaśipu, Jamba, Maya, and others of immense ascetic fervor. / The greatly valiant Makara went to the world of Brahmā.
Having deluded Brahmā, that powerful one seized the Vedas. / And having swallowed the sacred revelation, he then entered the great ocean.
Then the entire universe became empty, and there was a confusion of dharma: / no recitation of the Veda, no vaṣaṭ-call, devoid of castes and life stages.
Then the god Brahmā, the lord of creatures, surrounded by all the hosts of gods, / went to the ocean of milk and, taking refuge, praised the God.
Brahmā said: / Be gracious, O God, my master, resting upon the serpent-couch! / O Lord of all, Self of all gods, Acyuta composed of all the Vedas!
You are the primal seed of the universe of the earth; in the middle, you are greater than everything; / and at the end, you are the lord of creatures, and by your own will, you are darkness itself.
You alone uphold the entire eternal universe whose form is consciousness. / For you are the unmanifest, the origin of elements, the primordial nature, the imperishable person.
Your form is the beginning, middle, and end of the universe, O Supreme Lord! / You alone are the refuge of all the worlds, O Puruṣottama!
You are the origin of elements, the great being, the cause of the aggregate of beings. / Taking recourse in that very cause, the self-possessed one delights in his abode.
You are the primary being and you are the end; you are the wind, all-pervading and great; / you are the beginning and you are without beginning; you are fire, the receptacle of splendors.
You are the waters, the life of all the worlds, O Supreme Lord! / You are the earth, the support of the universe; you are the mountain-bearer, O greatly wise one!
You indeed are the river and the ocean, and you alone are the beginning of everything. / You alone are the divine sage, all living beings, O Puruṣottama!
Prompted by you alone, people act among good and bad [deeds]. / Oppressed by the Daitya, the Vedas have entered the great ocean.
All this moving and unmoving universe has the Vedas as its support, / and the foundation of all righteous duties rests entirely on the Vedas.
In the Vedas lies the constant satisfaction of all the gods. / Therefore, you alone are worthy to bring back the Vedas, O Keśava!
Śrī Mahādeva said: / Thus addressed by Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Lord, / assuming the form of a fish, entered the great ocean.
Assuming a fish's shape, he split with the tip of his snout that very fierce Daitya, / who was worshiped by the gods, and then struck him down.
Having killed him, that god of great splendor took all the Vedas / along with their auxiliary sciences and sub-limbs, and handed them over to Brahmā.
The Vedas, swallowed by that Rākṣasa, had become intermingled with one another; / they were made distinct by that wise Lord in the form of Vyāsa.
The Vedas were thus separated all together by the great-souled Vyāsa. / In this way all the deities were protected by the Fish incarnation.

Having freed the three worlds from anguish at that time by bestowing the sacred revelation, Hari, / whose feet were worshiped by yogins, praised by hosts of gods and Siddhas, vanished— / indeed the venerable Vāsudeva, Hari, composed of all gods.

6.231.m: Śrī Rudra said: / That Tortoise manifestation of Viṣṇu, worshiped by all the worlds, / I shall describe, my dear; listen with concentrated mind.
The son of Atri, renowned as Durvāsas, possessed great splendor; / he was fierce, a shaker of all the worlds, of great ascetic fervor.
That Brahmarṣi, a treasure of ascetic fervor, an emanation of myself, / an object of fear to everyone always, went to the slopes of the Himavat mountain.
Having resided there for a year, worshiped by the Kinnara maidens, / that sage, desiring to see the great Indra, set out for heaven.
At that time, that one of great splendor saw the lord mounted on an elephant, / Śacī's husband, being worshiped by all the gods.
Seeing that, Durvāsas, of very great ascetic fervor, with a delighted mind, / presented him with a garland of pārijāta flowers, full of humility.
Taking that garland and placing it on the head of his elephant, / the lord of deities, the lord of gods, set out toward the Nandana garden.
Then the elephant, intoxicated with rut, seized that garland with its trunk, / crushed it, and threw it down upon the surface of the earth.
Then the greatly splendid Durvāsas, red-eyed with rage, / tormented by the fire of anger, cursed that great Indra.
Durvāsas said: / Because, filled with the supreme majesty of the three worlds, you disrespect me, / therefore may the majesty of the three worlds be ruined, without a doubt!
Rudra said: / Thus cursed, Śakra then went back to his own city. / Thereupon Śrī, the bearer of the worlds, herself vanished in an instant.
When Lakṣmī vanished, the three worlds were immediately ruined— / she, on whose sidelong glance the entire universe, moving and unmoving, depends.
When she disappeared, everything fell into greater ruin: / all the thirty [gods] headed by Brahmā, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras,
Daityas, Dānavas, Nāgas, humans, and Rākṣasas as well, / beasts, birds, worms, all immobile and mobile beings.
Since that Lakṣmī, the mother of the world, did not look upon them, / they were all overtaken by poverty and became partakers of misery.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, the gods cried out, robbed of their senses; / the cloud did not rain, and all reservoirs of water dried up.
All the trees dried up, devoid of fruit and flowers. / Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas,
afflicted by hunger and thirst, went to Brahmā of unmeasured splendor; / they spoke to that god, lord of gods, the lotus-born grandfather.
The gods said: / "O Blessed One, the three worlds are afflicted indeed by hunger and thirst; / no oblation is made, nor the vaṣaṭkāra call; [the world] is devoid of all dharma.
All gods, Dānavas, and humans are afflicted by hunger and thirst; / they have gone for refuge to you, the savior, the lord of all the worlds.
You ought to save these people afflicted by hunger and thirst, O lord of gods!" / Rudra said: Having heard their speech, the grandfather of all the worlds,
highly pleased, said to them all, conferring honor: / Brahmā said: "Listen, all you deities, Daityas, Gandharvas, and humans!
Through the transgression of Mahendra all this has occurred; / this dreadful, great ruin of the world has arisen,
because the great-souled Durvāsas incurred anger; / through his anger, O gods, this triad of worlds has been ruined.
His mind seized by indignation, corrupted by wrath, / that foolish [Indra] was told: 'May the three worlds be stripped of fortune!'
From that curse, Lakṣmī, the supporter of the worlds and beloved of Nārāyaṇa, / the goddess, the mother of the world, the supreme sovereign, vanished.
When worlds are looked upon by her side-glance, they become happy; / when not looked upon by the mother of the world, they are indeed only partakers of misery.
Therefore let us all go and worship in the Milk Ocean / that eternal god Nārāyaṇa who abides there, the supreme one.
When that lord of gods is pleased, this world will be auspicious." / Having resolved thus in his mind, Brahmā, joined by the hosts of gods
together with Bhrgu and other sages, went to the Ocean of Milk. / On the northern shore of the Milk Ocean, the deities headed by Brahmā and Rudra
worshiped Viṣṇu properly with the Puruṣa hymn, / muttering the eight-syllable mantra and the Puruṣasūkta.
Meditating with undivided minds, they offered oblations to the Supreme Lord; / they praised him with celestial hymns and bowed in various ways.
Then the Blessed One, pleased with all the dwellers of heaven, / stood within their sight, being praised by the great sages,
having mounted the son of Vinatā, the all-pervading lord who embodies all the gods. / Beholding that lord of the worlds, holding the conch, discus, and mace,
dressed in yellow garments, four-armed, with eyes resembling white lotuses, / his chest adorned with the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, decorated with a forest garland,
beautified with a diadem, necklaces, armlets, and anklets, / they praised him with cries of victory and bowed down constantly.
Then the Blessed One graciously spoke to all the deities; / he said: "I am a granter of boons; choose a boon, O gods!"
Having heard this, all the gods then, preceded by Brahmā, / with joined palms spoke these words to God, the Lord:
The gods said: / "O Blessed One, because of the sage's curse, this entire triad of worlds, / along with gods, asuras, and humans, is now afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Therefore, O Puruṣottama, we have sought refuge in you; / save this whole world; no one else can be capable anywhere."
Rudra said: Being thus addressed by all the deities, Acyuta, the Supreme Lord, / having considered this, said to those gods headed by Brahmā:
The Blessed One said: "Because of the curse of the sage, the son of Atri, Ramā vanished; / by her side-glance the world was endowed with sovereignty.
Therefore, all you gods headed by Śiva and Brahmā, / uprooting Mount Mandara and placing it in the Milk Ocean,
making Mandara the churning stick, wound round by the king of serpents, / perform the churning, O gods, along with the Daityas, Gandharvas, and Dānavas!
That Lakṣmī will arise for the protection of the world; / delighted by her, you fortunate ones will prosper, of this there is no doubt.
I myself shall support the mountain, assuming the form of a tortoise; / and entering all the gods through my power, I shall make them stronger."
Rudra said: Being thus addressed by Hari, O woman of lovely signs, / all the deities headed by Brahmā said to the lord of gods: "Excellent! Excellent!"
Being praised by the foremost of the gods, the glorious, imperishable Lord, / bowed to by all the worlds, the support of all, the God of all, looking equally upon everything, then vanished.

6.232.m:
Śaṅkara said:
Then all the hosts of gods and the mighty Dānavas and others
uprooted Mount Mandara and cast it into the ocean.

Then glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, the creator of beings,
of immeasurable prowess, supported that mountain in the form of a tortoise.

Having a body without beginning, middle, or end, the eternal Lord of the universe,
possessing all forms and worthy of worship, held up the best of mountains.

Likewise with a single arm, the all-pervading, imperishable Lord [supported it].
Then all the gods and Asuras churned the ocean of milk,

wrapping Mount Mandara with the king of serpents so that it whirled noisily.
Then, as the milk ocean was being churned by the extremely powerful deities,

all the great seers, for the purpose of the manifestation of Lakṣmī,
fasted, observed disciplines, and chanted the Śrīsūkta.

The best among the twice-born recited the Thousand Names [of Viṣṇu].
On the pure eleventh lunar day, while the great ocean was being churned,

all the seers, having fasted, chanted the supreme mantra of Śrī.
And those who desired to chant to Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and Hari,

the eminent twice-born, the best of sages, meditated upon them and worshipped them.
Then, at that auspicious moment, as the great ocean was being churned,

there arose first the great poison Kālakūṭa,
causing immense torment, extremely terrible, brilliant like the fire of cosmic dissolution.

Seeing it, all the gods and Dānavas fled, afflicted with fear.
Then, seeing those best of gods fleeing in terror,

I spoke these words to them there, O fair-eyed one:
“O hosts of gods, none of you should fear the poison.

I shall consume this great poison Kālakūṭa.”
When addressed thus by me, all the gods headed by Indra,

bowing down deeply, praised me with the words, “Well done! Well done!”
Seeing that great poison arise, resembling a dark cloud,

and meditating in my heart upon Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose banner bears Garuḍa,
who resembles the rising sun, and holds the conch, discus, and mace,

the Lord accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, wearing earrings of molten gold,
meditating with single-pointed mind upon the Lord who removes all sorrow,

and chanting the great mantra consisting of his names accompanied by Lakṣmī,
that extremely dreadful, primal poison that caused fear to all,

by the power of the three names of the all-pervading Viṣṇu,
that poison capable of destroying the worlds was digested.

The three names of Hari, namely “Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda”:
he who, disciplined and devoted, chants them, preceded by Om and ending with namaḥ,

has no great fear of death, poison, disease, or fire.
Whoever, self-controlled, chants the great mantra of the three names

has no fear of death or Time, nor anything else.
Thus, by the three names alone, O goddess, was the poison drunk by me.

Then the thirty [gods], delighted and astonished, praised me.
Bowing to me, the gods once more churned the ocean of milk.
As it was being churned by me and the gods, O passionate woman,

the goddess Jyeṣṭhā appeared, adorned with a garland of gems and garments.
Upon appearing, she said to the gods: “What should I do?”

All the hosts of gods spoke emphatically to that goddess.
The gods said:
“In whose pleasant homes quarreling occurs,

that place we assign to you; dwell there, accompanied by inauspiciousness!
Those who speak harshly and constantly utter falsehoods,

and those wicked ones of impure mind who sleep at twilight—
reside in their homes, bringing misery and poverty!

Where there are skull fragments, hair, ashes, bones, chaff, and charcoal,
there will be your permanent dwelling without a doubt.

In whose house there are skulls, bones, ashes, hair, and such marks,
dwell there, O inauspicious one, constantly along with Kali!

That fool who sips water for purification without first washing his feet—
cleave to him, O great goddess, who is thoroughly enveloped in impurity!

Vile men who clean their teeth with chaff, charcoal, potsherds, stones,
sand, cloth, or leather—

delight with Kali in their homes forever, O goddess!
Those vile men who eat sesame paste, kalañja, kaliga, śigru, and garlic,

mushrooms, village pig, bilva fruit, kośātakī fruit,
gourd, and onion—
in their house let your residence always be, O goddess, granter of poverty!”

Rudra said:
Having thus instructed Jyeṣṭhā, the beloved of Kali, all the gods,
with minds fully collected, again churned the ocean of milk.

Then the goddess Vāruṇī arose, O fair-faced one;
and the serpent-king Ananta took the fair-eyed one.

Then Surā arose, adorned with all ornaments;
she became the wife of Garuḍa, graced with all auspicious marks.

Then the divine hosts of Apsarases and the Gandharvas of great splendor
were born, endowed with beauty and devoted to sweet singing.

Then Airāvata was born, as was the horse Uccaiḥśravas,
Dhanvantari, the Pārijāta tree, and the wish-fulfilling cow Surabhi.

The thousand-eyed [Indra] took all of these with a delighted heart.
Then, at daybreak on the twelfth lunar day when the sun rose,

as it was being churned again by the gods led by Indra,
praised with cheerful faces by the great seers,

there arose auspicious Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of all the worlds,
resembling ten million rising suns, adorned with golden armlets,

seated on a golden lotus, graced with all auspicious marks,
with eyes wide like lotus petals, and dark, curly hair,

her limbs smeared with divine sandalwood, adorned with celestial flowers,
endowed with all heavenly ornaments made of various gems,

slender-waisted, the nurse of the universe, with full, elevated breasts,
four-armed, large-eyed, her face like the full moon,

holding a vessel of wealth, a citron, and a pair of auspicious golden lotuses
with her lotus hands adorned with all kinds of jewelry,

wearing a garland of unfading lotuses upon her chest.
They beheld that great goddess who desires the welfare of all the worlds,

the ruler of all beings, the mother wearing a garland of lotuses,
Nārāyaṇī, the nurse of the universe, residing in the heart of Nārāyaṇa.

Seeing Mahālakṣmī, all the deities were delighted;
the hosts of gods in heaven beat their drums loudly.

Forest goddesses showered continuous showers of flowers;
lords of the Gandharvas sang, and hosts of Apsarases danced.

Auspicious breezes blew; the sun shone with great brilliance;
calm fires burned brightly; and the ten directions grew serene.

Immediately afterward, the cool-rayed one arose in the milk ocean,
Soma, possessing nectar-filled rays, the brother of the Mother, who brings joy,

and the Moon became the ruler of constellations, the maternal uncle of the worlds.
Then the sacred wife of Hari, Tulasī, who purifies the worlds,

the nurse of the universe, was born for the worship of Hari, wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then all the gods, the dwellers of heaven, had their minds filled with joy.
Having set up that mountain as before, their desires fully attained, / all the gods, led by Śiva and Brahmā, approached the Mother.
Having praised her with the thousand names, they recited the collections of the Śrīsūkta. / Then that goddess, being pleased, spoke to all the gods:
Śrī said: / 'Choose a boon, best of gods; good fortune to you! I am the granter of boons.' / Rudra said: / With folded hands, their bodies bowed, the gods said to Śrī:
The gods said: / 'Be gracious, O goddess Kamalā, beloved of the Lord of all the worlds! / O goddess, remain forever inseparable upon Viṣṇu's chest!
Protect the three worlds, O goddess, eternal Supreme Mistress! / The entire world, both moving and unmoving, depends upon your side-glance.
Looked upon by you, all the gods thrive. / You are the mother of the gods beginning with Rudra; sovereignty arises from your glance.
This is what we desire, O goddess, Mother of the World; salutations to you!' / Rudra said: / Having been thus addressed by all the deities, the Great Mistress, Mother of the World,
Nārāyaṇa's beloved, said to those gods, 'So be it!' / Then Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
appeared just so, as before, in the ocean of milk, as did Brahmā. / Thereupon the gods praised him, having bowed down to Janārdana.
All of them, with folded hands and joyful faces, spoke auspiciously: / The gods said: / 'O Lord of all, take as your beloved the goddess, the Great Fortune,
Lakṣmī, who never departs, for the sake of protecting the world.' / Rudra said: / Having spoken thus, all the gods together with the sages, headed by Brahmā,
overflowing with tears of joy, placed the goddess and the god / upon a heavenly seat made of diverse jewels, resembling the rising sun.
With heavenly garments, divine garlands, and adorned with various gems, / they worshipped Acyuta, who was seated together with Lakṣmī,
and they worshipped the Supreme Mistress with perfumes, incenses, lamps, / offerings made of nectar, and extraordinary divine fruits.
The goddess Tulasī, tender and auspicious, had arisen from the nectar; / with her they swiftly worshipped the pair of feet of the Lord of Śrī.
Having made three circumambulations and bowed down again and again, / the gods praised them with hymns, overcome with tears of joy.
Then the blessed Hari, the lord, sovereign of all the gods, being pleased, / granted them their desired boons together with the goddess.

Then the gods, humans, and others, exceedingly joyful, purified by the sight bestowed by Lakṣmī's side-glance, / endowed with abundant grain and wealth, attained perpetual, supreme, and completely disease-free happiness.

6.233.m:
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, named the Origin of Lakṣmī, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

Thus [ends the chapter] named the Narration of the Fasting on the Eleventh Day, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.234.m: Pārvatī said: / 'O Blessed One, I wish to hear the ordinance of the twelfth lunar day, / and the rite of Viṣṇu's worship that must be performed on it, O Lord,
and the power of the eleventh lunar day, which removes all sins of mortals; / declare it thus in detail out of love for me, O Maheśvara.'
Mahādeva said: / 'Listen, O goddess; I will proclaim the ordinance of the twelfth lunar day, / merely by the remembrance of which Janārdana becomes pleased.
When the eleventh lunar day arrives, humans who fast on it in this world, / freed from all sins, go to Viṣṇu's supreme abode.
Sin acquired across seven lifetimes, committed knowingly or unknowingly, / goes to destruction in an instant by worshipping Hari on the twelfth lunar day.
Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices / are not worth a sixteenth part of a fast on the eleventh lunar day.
For indeed it grants dharma, grants wealth, grants desires, and grants liberation; / the twelfth lunar day yields all desires for mortals, O fair-complexioned one.
There is no protection against sin equal to the eleventh lunar day; / there is no observance equal to the eleventh lunar day, O auspicious-eyed one.
Whoever, abandoning the eleventh lunar day, observes another vow / abandons a great kingdom resting in his hand and begs for alms.
Whatever sin has been committed by the eleven senses, O beloved, / all of that dissolves through fasting on the eleventh lunar day.
The Purāṇas repeatedly proclaim aloud in this world, O lovely-faced one: / "One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari arrives!"
[Food] is always declared inedible [then]; how much more in both the bright and dark fortnights / for all castes and stages of life, O fair-complexioned one!'
The fast on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) must indeed be performed, there is no doubt about this; / and when the eleventh day arrives on the day of the death of one's mother or father,
[the funeral offering] must be made on the twelfth day, never on the day of fasting. / For the ancestors and the dwellers of heaven do not eat condemned food.
One must not eat on the eleventh day, nor ever drink liquor, / nor kill a brāhmaṇa—these three are considered equal.
Therefore, one should observe a fast on the pure eleventh day, / striving with speech, body, and actions in all three states.
One should diligently avoid [an Ekādaśī] mixed with the tenth day. / If it is mixed with the tenth day at the time of dawn,
abandoning that, one should fast on the pure twelfth day here without hesitation. / When even a single digit exists toward sunrise,
and likewise, O goddess, the twelfth day extends into the thirteenth day, / then the pure twelfth day is enjoined for the fast.
At the time of dawn one should perform all the requisite rites; / breaking the fast is also prescribed there while a digit of the twelfth day remains.
One should also abandon a pure eleventh day here, without doubt, / where even a digit of the eleventh day remains on the twelfth day when the sun rises.
Leaving aside the entire eleventh day, a twice-born should fast on that very [twelfth day]. / Having thus determined the rule, Hari's day should be fasted upon.
[Abandoning] the evening meal on the first of those days, and the evening and morning [meals] on the middle day— / one should fast there having given up the four meals.
On the tenth day one should eat once, refrain from union with women, / sleep on the ground, and on the next day dwell pure.
With his limbs smeared with myrobalan fruit, he should perform his bath and twilight prayers. / Devoted to the fast, he should worship Hari at night.
A heretic, one engaged in wrongful deeds, an outcaste, and an outcaste dog-cooker— / a Vaiṣṇava should not look upon, converse with, or touch them on that occasion.
A brāhmaṇa who is not a Vaiṣṇava is declared to be a heretic; / and one who abandons the topknot and sacred thread is called one engaged in wrongful deeds.
One joined with great sins or minor sins is called an outcaste; / a low-caste person is called a dog-cooker; such is the well-founded conclusion according to the Vedas.
Having worshipped the Lord of gods at night, he should keep a vigil / with perfumes, flowers, lamps, garments, and auspicious ornaments,
and worship with devotion at night through recitations, hymns of praise, and obeisances. / Then, at dawn, with waters mixed with tulasī,
having bathed properly according to the rule and gratified the ancestors and deities, / he should worship Janārdana, the Lord of the worlds, together with Lakṣmī,
with tender tulasī leaves and fragrant flowers. / There he should wave lamps one hundred and eight times;
he should properly offer the two of them a garland made of lotuses. / He should offer incense, a lamp, food offering, and betel;
he should offer divine milk-rice mixed with sugar, / and offer betel combined with camphor.
Having performed circumambulation and obeisance endowed with devotion, / he should likewise offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire one hundred and eight times,
with each verse of the Puruṣasūkta, and [offer] milk-rice with the Lakṣmīsūkta. / He should feed brāhmaṇas with devotion, and himself eat with restrained speech.
He should spend that great day in reciting the Purāṇas and other texts; / sleeping on the ground, celibate, he should sleep on that very night.
Being thus worshipped on the twelfth day, the Lord, the husband of Kamalā, / is pleased in an instant and surely grants all desires.
Thus has this supreme observance of the twelfth day been told, O goddess; / what else do you wish to hear that must be spoken? That I shall declare.

6.235.m: Śrī Pārvatī said: / As to what was said by you, 'One should avoid conversation with heretics,'

which was declared to me here, O Lord, as even more despicable than a dog-cooker: / of what nature are they declared to be, and by what signs are they marked on earth? / Rudra said: / Those who, deluded by ignorance, proclaim another deity to be supreme,
apart from Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the world, are considered heretics. / Those who carry a skull, ashes, and bones, and who bear non-Vedic insignia,
